_readme: A fixed corpus and twelve hand-labelled procurement queries.
Labels are relevance judgements about the article, not predictions about what the
retriever can find. A German article about a port strike is relevant to the English
query 'port strike' whether or not lexical search can reach it — labelling around a
system's limitations is how an evaluation stops measuring anything.
Two cases expect no results at all. A system that always returns something is not
measurably better than one that returns nothing, and without these the floor could
be met by a retriever that answers every query with the whole corpus.
Article ids are stable strings; the harness maps them to database ids on load.
_floor_readme: Measured, not chosen. Established 2026-08-23 by running scripts/evaluate_search.py
against this corpus, then set a hair below the observed values so a float rounding
difference cannot fail a build while a real regression still does.
Two floors because CI can only run one of them. Hybrid retrieval needs an embedding
provider, and a build that spends money on every push and depends on a third party
being reachable is a build somebody eventually disables. CI gates lexical; run
`--hybrid` locally to check the whole stack.
Observed lexical: P@5 0.300, R@10 0.528, MRR 0.750, nDCG 0.573
Observed hybrid:  P@5 0.567, R@10 1.000, MRR 1.000, nDCG 0.988
A floor moves up when retrieval improves. Lowering one needs a note in the phase
plan saying what was traded away and why.
What the lexical gate cannot catch, established by trying it: reversing the result
order changes none of the four numbers. websearch_to_tsquery is AND across terms, so
most queries match only one or two documents and ordering has nothing to do. The
lexical gate catches matching regressions — disabling stemming drops it to P@5 0.233,
R@10 0.306, MRR 0.417, nDCG 0.328 — and is blind to ranking ones.
The hybrid floor does catch ranking: reversing fusion order holds recall at 1.000
while MRR falls to 0.409 and nDCG to 0.587. That gap is the argument for running
--hybrid before a release even though CI cannot.

cases.why: The plain risk phrasing. a02 says the same thing without either query word and a03 says it in German.
Multilingual. Stemming must reach Hafenstreiks from Hafenstreik; the English articles are on-topic regardless of what any retriever can do about it.
No single article contains both words in its title, which is what makes this a recall test rather than a lookup.
Vocabulary mismatch: buyers say chips, press releases say semiconductors.
Supplier name lookup, the most common query shape in this product.
D5's whole argument. Siemens AG is a different legal entity with a different risk profile, so a11 is not relevant and a retriever that returns it is wrong rather than merely imprecise.
The compliance-critical query. A miss here is a false negative in screening terms.
Purely semantic: shares no content word with a01 or a03.
Multi-term, where a15 is on-topic without naming the Red Sea.
Spelling variant. Stemming cannot rescue a typo, so this case measures what query understanding would buy — deliberately out of scope until it can be measured.
Correct answer is nothing. Vector retrieval will always have a nearest neighbour, so this only passes with a distance threshold.
The second no-result case, phrased as an ordinary sentence rather than nonsense words, so it cannot be caught by an out-of-vocabulary shortcut.
